(2019) Predicting engagement with an online psychosocial intervention for psychosis: exploring individual- and intervention-level predictors. *Internet Interventions*, 18: 100266. sources.population: adults 18-65 with a SCID-confirmed nonorganic psychotic disorder in the past 2 years, recruited through community mental health services and Facebook, Victoria, Australia
sources.perspective: clinical psychology and digital mental health / secondary analysis of randomised conditions with website log data
sources.dataset: Self-Management and Recovery Technology (SMART) research programme, Australia
sources.title: Predicting engagement with an online psychosocial intervention for psychosis: Exploring individual- and intervention-level predictors
sources.strength_why: A prospective study of 98 adults with SCID-confirmed psychosis in which the key predictor, asynchronous email support, was randomised and engagement was measured objectively from website logs rather than self-report, so it can establish that light-touch human support raises use of a self-guided online intervention in this population and that externally controlled motivation moderates that effect. It cannot establish that more use produces better clinical outcomes, because no outcome was measured here and the authors say the dose-response relationship may not be linear; nor can it generalise to routine care, because the sample was research-recruited, internet-confident and screened. Moderate rather than strong: the randomised comparison is sound but the sample is small, the predictor set was analysed observationally, and one table is internally inconsistent (see Limitations).

(2018) Childhood trauma is associated with severity of hallucinations and delusions in psychotic disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *Schizophrenia Bulletin*, 44 (5): 1111-1122. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbx161 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 4680 participants with a diagnosed psychotic disorder, pooled from 29 meta-analysed studies out of 41 meeting inclusion criteria
sources.perspective: clinical psychology / systematic review and meta-analysis of correlational studies
sources.title: Childhood trauma is associated with severity of hallucinations and delusions in psychotic disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A systematic review screening 6667 studies to 41, meta-analysing 29 with 4680 participants, with reporting bias and quality assessed and unpublished data sought from authors. It moves the trauma argument one step past risk of onset — which Varese et al. (2012) already covers — to severity of specific symptoms: childhood trauma correlates with hallucination severity (r = .199) and delusion severity (r = .172), both P < .001. It also delivers a result the authors did NOT expect and report as such: trauma was not correlated with negative-symptom severity (r = .049, P = .095), while neglect specifically was (r = .142, P = .005). It CANNOT establish that trauma shapes the CONTENT of psychotic experience — severity is not content, and nothing here addresses what the voices or delusions are about. Nor can it establish direction: the pooled studies are correlational, and the effects are small (r around .17 to .20, roughly 3-4% of variance). Moderate on design, with a clear ceiling on what it may be asked to say.

sources.harvard: Birdsey, N. & Kustner, C. (2021) Reviewing the Social GRACES: what do they add and limit in systemic thinking and practice? *The American Journal of Family Therapy*, 49 (5): 429-442. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1080/01926187.2020.1830731 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: no participants; a review of the systemic-practice and family-therapy literature, with one illustrative clinical supervision case from UK practice
sources.perspective: systemic family therapy and clinical psychology / critical narrative review
sources.title: Reviewing the Social GRACES: What do they add and limit in systemic thinking and practice?
sources.strength_why: A peer-reviewed review that traces the Social GRACES to named origins — Burnham (1992, 1993) and Roper-Hall (1998), via the earlier 'DISGRRACCE' mnemonic — lists the current fifteen graces, and then sets out four substantive criticisms: that the framework is restrictively linear, that it is reductive and risks becoming 'a list of areas of difference', that therapists privilege the graces inside their own comfort zone, and that the current fifteen omit disablism. It can establish what the GRACES are, where they came from and what they are criticised for, which is exactly what a cultural-considerations paragraph needs. It CANNOT establish that using them changes clinical outcomes: there is no trial, no outcome measure and no psychosis population anywhere in it, and the single clinical illustration is one anonymised supervision case written up by the authors. Indicative on design.

sources.perspective: clinical psychiatry / retrospective chart review with logistic regression

sources.title: 'The algorithm is hacked': analysis of technology delusions in a modern-day cohort
sources.strength_why: A single-centre retrospective chart review of 228 adults with psychosis that supplies the only year-on-year trend estimate in the corpus for technology-themed delusional content, and rich verbatim description of its subtypes. It can establish that technology themes are common in a contemporary psychosis service and that they became more likely across 2016-2024 in this sample; it cannot establish population prevalence, cause, or that technology contributed to the delusions, because the sample is a selected, housed, insured, substance-abstinent day-programme cohort and the data were never collected for research. The tier is held at moderate rather than higher by the design, by the authors' own point that rising clinician awareness could itself produce the trend, and by an unexplained discrepancy between the group sizes in Table 1 and the counts in the Results text (see Limitations).

sources.title: Delusion content across the 20th century in an American psychiatric hospital
sources.strength_why: A retrospective archival study of 102 records, sampled by decade from a single US state psychiatric hospital, which can show that delusional content in an American sample tracked sociocultural change in the same way non-American samples had. It cannot support any statement about frequency in a population, nor about technology specifically, because the sample is tiny per decade, confined to one institution, and the abstract reports no technology-specific result at all. Indicative rather than moderate because of the per-decade cell sizes and because the appraisal rests on the abstract alone.

sources.authors: Cantor-Graae, E. & Selten, J. P.
sources.harvard: Cantor-Graae, E. & Selten, J. P. (2005) Schizophrenia and migration: a meta-analysis and review. *American Journal of Psychiatry*, 162 (1): 12-24. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.162.1.12 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: population-based incidence studies of migrant groups, published 1977-2003; 40 effect sizes for first-generation migrants, 7 for second-generation, 50 in the combined analysis
sources.perspective: social psychiatry / meta-analysis of population-based incidence studies
sources.title: Schizophrenia and migration: a meta-analysis and review.
sources.strength_why: A mixed-effects meta-analysis of population-based incidence studies that established the size of the migrant excess in schizophrenia — relative risk 2.7 (95% CI 2.3-3.2) for first-generation and 4.5 (95% CI 1.5-13.1) for second-generation migrants — and found it graded by the migrant group's region of origin and skin colour, which is the finding that pushed the field towards psychosocial rather than genetic explanations. It cannot establish causation and the second-generation estimate rests on only 7 effect sizes with an interval from 1.5 to 13.1. Moderate rather than strong because the search was MEDLINE-only, English-language-only, and now over twenty years out of date; its figures are superseded by later reviews and it should be cited as the foundational finding rather than the current estimate.

sources.harvard: Ceraso, A., Lin, J. J., Schneider-Thoma, J., Siafis, S., Tardy, M., Komossa, K., Heres, S., Kissling, W., Davis, J. M. & Leucht, S. (2020) Maintenance treatment with antipsychotic drugs for schizophrenia. *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews*, 8 (8): CD008016. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD008016.pub3 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 9145 participants in 75 randomised controlled trials comparing maintenance antipsychotic medication with placebo in schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like psychoses; trials published 1959 to 2017, size 14 to 420 participants
sources.perspective: psychopharmacology / Cochrane systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and GRADE
sources.dataset: Cochrane Schizophrenia Group Study-Based Register of Trials
sources.title: Maintenance treatment with antipsychotic drugs for schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A Cochrane review of 75 placebo-controlled RCTs and 9145 participants with GRADE certainty ratings, reporting the relapse-prevention effect as high-certainty evidence: 24% relapse on drug versus 61% on placebo at seven to twelve months (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.45, NNTB 3), with hospitalisation reduced from 18% to 7% (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.57, NNTB 8). It also quantifies the harms in the same currency — movement disorders 14% versus 8% (RR 1.52, NNTH 20), sedation and weight gain — which is what makes it usable for a shared decision rather than an argument for medication. It CANNOT answer the vignette's actual question: the population is schizophrenia broadly rather than first episode, the evidence runs 'approximately up to two years of follow-up' and no further, the suicide and employment analyses are underpowered and low-certainty, and randomisation, allocation and blinding were 'poorly reported' in many included studies. Strong on design and on the authors' own GRADE rating of the primary outcome.

sources.authors: Chadwick, P., Williams, C. & Mackenzie, J.
team: University of Southampton / Royal South Hants Hospital (Chadwick)
sources.harvard: Chadwick, P., Williams, C. & Mackenzie, J. (2003) Impact of case formulation in cognitive behaviour therapy for psychosis. *Behaviour Research and Therapy*, 41 (6): 671-680. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/S0005-7967(02)00033-5 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: people receiving cognitive behaviour therapy for psychosis, Southampton, UK; sample size not stated in the abstract
sources.perspective: clinical psychology / two within-subject experiments around a therapy component
sources.title: Impact of case formulation in cognitive behaviour therapy for psychosis.
sources.strength_why: The only empirical test of case formulation in psychosis I could locate, and it is a largely NULL and partly adverse result: across two experiments, formulation 'had little or no impact' on perceived therapeutic relationship, on strength of delusional and self-evaluative beliefs, or on anxiety and depression; therapists' own ratings of the relationship improved while clients' did not, and six clients found formulation at least in part a negative experience. It can therefore establish that a formulation-led plan should not be presented as an intervention with demonstrated benefit, which is a real constraint on `e2-plan`. It CANNOT establish that formulation is useless — it is small, uncontrolled, single-site, from one service, over twenty years old and predates the Five Ps version of the framework, and the abstract does not report the sample size. Indicative on design; its FIT to the claim that a formulation-based plan is justified is high precisely because it qualifies it.

U. *et al.* (2018) Comparison of early intervention services vs treatment as usual for early-phase psychosis: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression. *JAMA Psychiatry*, 75 (6): 555-565. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2018.0623 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 2176 patients in 10 randomised clinical trials of first-episode psychosis or early-phase schizophrenia spectrum disorder; mean age 27.5 years (SD 4.6), 1355 (62.3%) male; trial duration mean 16.2 months (SD 7.4), range 9-24 months
sources.perspective: psychiatry and health services research / systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression
sources.title: Comparison of early intervention services vs treatment as usual for early-phase psychosis: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-reported systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 RCTs and 2176 patients, with prespecified subgroup and meta-regression analyses and unpublished data obtained from the authors of every included trial, reporting risk ratios and standardised mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. It is the best available evidence that a coordinated multimodal service — not any single modality — outperforms ordinary care in early-phase psychosis, and its inclusion criteria define that service as combining psychosocial AND psychopharmacological components delivered by one team, which is the direct evidence that a plan touching several domains beats a referral chain. It CANNOT establish which component does the work: the unit of randomisation is the service, so the meta-analysis is silent on the contribution of medication, family work, vocational support or psychotherapy taken separately. It also cannot speak beyond 24 months, the longest trial duration included, and the protocol was 'predetermined but unpublished' rather than registered, which is a transparency weakness in an otherwise well-conducted review.

sources.perspective: clinical psychiatry / systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of observational studies
sources.title: Prenatal and perinatal risk and protective factors for psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered (CRD42017079261) systematic review and meta-analysis of 152 non-overlapping cohort and case-control datasets covering 98 candidate factors, with random-effects pairwise meta-analyses, correction for publication bias, sensitivity analyses, meta-regressions and a study-quality assessment. It can establish which prenatal and perinatal exposures are reliably associated with later psychosis and how large each association is. It cannot establish causation or mechanism, and because almost every individual odds ratio is small — most between 1.2 and 1.9 — it cannot support a strong single-factor neurodevelopmental claim.

sources.population: 901 patients aged 18-64 with first-episode psychosis presenting to psychiatric services, and 1237 population controls, across 11 sites in Europe and Brazil
sources.perspective: psychiatric epidemiology / multicentre incidence-linked case-control with population attributable fractions
sources.title: The contribution of cannabis use to variation in the incidence of psychotic disorder across Europe (EU-GEI): a multicentre case-control study.
sources.strength_why: A multicentre first-episode case-control study (901 cases, 1237 population controls) across 11 sites, which links individual-level exposure to site-level incidence and so does something a single-site case-control cannot: it tests whether differences in cannabis use patterns track differences in incidence between places. It can establish a graded association by frequency and potency and estimate how much of the incidence at each site is attributable to high-potency use. It cannot establish causation — the population attributable fractions are explicitly calculated 'assuming causality' — and the site-level correlations rest on only 11 data points.

sources.harvard: Fisher, M., Holland, C., Subramaniam, K. & Vinogradov, S. (2010) Neuroplasticity-based cognitive training in schizophrenia: an interim report on the effects 6 months later. *Schizophrenia Bulletin*, 36 (4): 869-879. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbn170 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 32 clinically stable adults with schizophrenia, recruited in San Francisco, USA (UCSF and San Francisco VA Medical Center)
sources.perspective: clinical neuroscience / randomised controlled trial with 6-month follow-up
sources.title: Neuroplasticity-based cognitive training in schizophrenia: An interim report on the effects 6 months later.
sources.strength_why: A randomised trial, which is the strongest DESIGN in this part of the corpus, but an interim report on 32 participants split unevenly between arms (22 training, 10 computer-games control), with the training arm itself split 12/10 by dose. It can establish that durable cognitive gains at 6 months after neuroplasticity-based training are demonstrable and that the direction of effect favours training. It cannot establish efficacy at any useful precision: the arms are far too small, the authors describe it as interim and ongoing, and the functional-outcome improvement is explicitly non-significant. Tier is indicative, not moderate, because of sample size and interim status, not because of design. Sixteen years old, and the training software has been superseded, so it is FOUNDATIONAL for the mechanism and not current for efficacy.

sources.perspective: clinical psychology / narrative review of early-intervention trials
sources.title: Cognitive interventions targeting brain plasticity in the prodromal and early phases of schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: An invited Annual Review that can establish the standard conceptual apparatus of early intervention — prodrome, clinical high risk, ultra high risk, duration of untreated psychosis, Birchwood's 'critical period' — with the terms attributed to their originators, and can summarise the state of cognitive therapy and cognitive training trials as of 2013. It cannot carry any prevalence, transition-rate or efficacy figure as current: it is thirteen years old and this corpus already holds Salazar de Pablo et al. (2021) on CHR transition, which supersedes it on that number. Tier is indicative: authoritative narrative review, no primary data, no systematic search.

sources.population: 18 827 children born in the UK in 2000-2001, Millennium Cohort Study, sampled at birth and at 9 months, 3, 5, 7 and 11 years
sources.perspective: economics and social epidemiology / longitudinal birth cohort analysis
sources.title: Poverty dynamics and parental mental health: Determinants of childhood mental health in the UK.
sources.strength_why: A large national birth cohort followed to age 11, which is a genuinely longitudinal design and therefore scarce in this corpus. It can establish that both persistent and transitory poverty are associated with all four SDQ domains at ages 5 and 11, with somewhat stronger estimated associations for persistent poverty, and that parental mental health is a major correlate. It CANNOT establish anything about psychosis: the outcome is the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire and the related Rutter scale, which screen for hyperactivity, emotional symptoms, conduct problems and peer problems, and the cohort is far too young for psychosis onset. It also cannot establish causation, being observational. Tier is moderate on quality; its FIT for a psychosis essay is POOR.

sources.perspective: digital psychiatry and lived experience / conceptual typology
sources.title: Beyond artificial intelligence psychosis: a functional typology of large language model-associated psychotic phenomena
sources.strength_why: A peer-reviewed Lancet Digital Health Viewpoint that proposes the catalyst / amplifier / coauthor / object typology for how LLM systems figure in psychotic phenomena, co-written by a software engineer, a person with lived experience of schizophrenia and a psychiatrist. It can establish where the typology comes from and what each category means; it cannot establish that the four roles are exhaustive, mutually exclusive or empirically distinguishable, because it reports no data and the illustrative cases are drawn from press accounts. Indicative rather than weak because it is peer reviewed in a major venue and has already been applied as a coding scheme by an independent team.

Available from: https://doi.org/10.1192/bjp.186.5.427 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: non-clinical adults, mostly students e-mailed at King's College London, University of East Anglia and University College London, United Kingdom
sources.perspective: clinical psychology / cross-sectional internet questionnaire survey
sources.title: Psychological investigation of the structure of paranoia in a non-clinical population
sources.strength_why: A large (n=1202) multidimensional questionnaire survey that established the continuum position for paranoia: the count of suspicious thoughts followed a single continuous, near-exponential distribution with no distinct subpopulation, and rarer, odder suspicions sat on top of commoner emotional concerns in a hierarchy. It can establish that paranoid thinking is common and continuously distributed in a non-clinical population and that it is structured rather than random; it cannot establish prevalence in any general population, nor causal direction, because the sample is a self-selected student convenience sample recruited by e-mail and the design is cross-sectional — both of which the authors state. Moderate rather than strong because of the sampling, not the analysis.

sources.harvard: Gao, Q., Zhu, P. & Hu, H. (2026) Factors associated with aggressive behavior in patients with schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *BMC Psychology*, 14 (1): 154. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03936-x (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 5096 patients diagnosed with schizophrenia by ICD-10, DSM-IV, DSM-5 or CCMD-3 (1766 aggressive, 3330 non-aggressive) across 24 studies in inpatient, outpatient and community settings
sources.perspective: public health / PRISMA meta-analysis of case-control and cross-sectional studies
sources.title: Factors associated with aggressive behavior in patients with schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered (CRD420251147415), PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis searching ten databases, six English and four Chinese (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, CBM), 2014 to October 2024, with Newcastle-Ottawa quality scoring (mostly 7-9 of 9), sensitivity and subgroup analyses, and funnel plots. It can establish the strength of association between a defined set of correlates and aggression in people already diagnosed with schizophrenia, with pooled odds ratios and confidence intervals. It cannot establish causation or anything about the onset of psychosis: the authors state that the included studies were 'primarily case-control and cross-sectional studies, which limit causal inference regarding etiology', and the outcome 'aggressive behavior' had no standardised operational definition across the primary studies. Current, not foundational. Fit caveat, which matters more here than the tier: this is violence risk in established schizophrenia, a different construct and a different population from first-episode or clinical high-risk psychosis, so it cannot carry any predisposing-factor claim in Essay 1.

sources.population: 27 meta-analyses of studies of people with adverse childhood experiences, with and without psychiatric diagnosis; constituent study populations not aggregated by country in this review
sources.perspective: behavioural medicine and neuroendocrinology / systematic review of meta-analyses
sources.title: Neurobiology of early life adversity: A systematic review of meta-analyses towards an integrative account of its neurobiological trajectories to mental disorders.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 27 meta-analyses that can establish convergent neurobiological correlates of adverse childhood experiences across four previously separate literatures — HPA axis, inflammation, neuroimaging and genetics/epigenetics — and can establish that those correlates appear in people with and without a psychiatric diagnosis, which is a real and unusual finding. It cannot establish causation and the authors call for longitudinal work to do so; it is also a review of reviews, so it is three steps from any participant and inherits every constituent meta-analysis's bias. Its outcome is mental disorders in general, NOT psychosis, which limits its fit here. Tier is moderate: rigorous method, stated limitations, but an umbrella design on a non-specific outcome.

sources.perspective: register-based epidemiology / nationwide cohort with population attributable risk fractions and joinpoint trend analysis
sources.title: Association between cannabis use disorder and schizophrenia stronger in young males than in females.
sources.strength_why: A nationwide register cohort covering 6,907,859 people and 129,521,260 person-years with 45,327 incident schizophrenia cases, which effectively removes selection and recall bias from exposure and outcome measurement and is large enough to estimate sex- and age-stratified effects and population attributable fractions over fifty years. It can establish that the association between diagnosed cannabis use disorder and schizophrenia is graded by sex and age and has grown over time. It cannot establish causation, and the exposure is a recorded diagnosis of cannabis use disorder rather than cannabis use, so it captures the severe tail of use and nothing below it.

sources.population: not applicable — Viewpoint, no participants
sources.perspective: phenomenological psychiatry / conceptual viewpoint
sources.title: Delusional Experiences Emerging From AI Chatbot Interactions or 'AI Psychosis'
sources.strength_why: A peer-reviewed Viewpoint in JMIR Mental Health that defines AI psychosis as a heuristic framework rather than a diagnostic entity and maps it onto the stress-vulnerability model, the digital therapeutic alliance and theory-of-mind accounts. It can establish how the term is used in the published literature and supply a conceptual vocabulary for a mechanism; it cannot establish that the mechanism operates, how often, or in whom, because it reports no data and the authors state the pathways are heuristic and make no causal claim. Indicative rather than weak because it is peer reviewed, explicitly scoped, and the authors are psychiatrists writing within established psychosis models, but it remains opinion rather than evidence.

sources.population: not applicable — course teaching slides, 9 slides
sources.perspective: clinical psychiatry teaching / course curriculum
sources.title: M6W4 – Evidence-Based Treatments for Complex Mental Health Conditions
sources.strength_why: Course teaching slides, unattributed to a named author, not peer reviewed and not publicly retrievable, so it cannot be cited as evidence for any claim in either essay — citing it would also be citing course notes, which the Module 3 brief explicitly asks students to distinguish from their own ideas and to reference properly. Its value is entirely as a SPECIFICATION of what the marker expects: it fixes the course's own wording of the 5Ps, of holistic formulation and of Verstehen, and it names the psychosis treatment list the assessment assumes. Every substantive point it makes must be re-sourced to a primary or secondary publication before it enters the essay. Tier is not-citable by definition of the venue, not by any defect in the content.

sources.population: no participants; mini-review of physical exercise and tDCS studies in schizophrenia
sources.perspective: clinical neuroscience / mini-review of adjunctive neuromodulation and exercise
sources.title: Enhancing neuroplasticity to augment cognitive remediation in schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A short mini-review, team-independent of the Vinogradov lineage, that can establish that response to cognitive remediation is highly variable, that combining it with exercise or tDCS is a live research strategy, and that the mechanistic rationale runs through BDNF and long-term potentiation. It cannot establish that the combination works: the authors state there are 'insufficient data to determine if this multimodal approach leads to incremental performance gain in patients' and call for larger RCTs. Nine years old and the tDCS literature has grown substantially since, so any claim about the state of that evidence must be dated. Tier is indicative: a mini-review with no primary data and explicitly insufficient evidence on its own question.

sources.harvard: Jauhar, S., McKenna, P. J., Radua, J., Fung, E., Salvador, R. & Laws, K. R. (2014) Cognitive-behavioural therapy for the symptoms of schizophrenia: systematic review and meta-analysis with examination of potential bias. *British Journal of Psychiatry*, 204 (1): 20-29. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1192/bjp.bp.112.116285 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 52 randomised trials of CBT for schizophrenia reported in 50 articles, searched 1993 to March 2013; participant countries not extracted
sources.perspective: psychiatry and clinical psychology / PRISMA systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis with moderator and publication-bias analysis
sources.title: Cognitive-behavioural therapy for the symptoms of schizophrenia: systematic review and meta-analysis with examination of potential bias
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of 52 randomised trials, pre-specified moderator analyses for three Cochrane risk-of-bias domains plus use of a control intervention, and three separate publication-bias tests: it is the primary source for every effect size the 2019 editorial reports, and it is the strongest treatment-efficacy source now in the corpus. It establishes that pooled end-of-treatment effects of CBT on overall, positive and negative symptoms in schizophrenia lie in the small range and that masking of outcome assessment significantly moderates them, with positive symptoms falling to non-significance in masked trials. Its own stated limits are real: the low-risk-of-bias subanalyses rest on 8-11 studies because most trials were rated 'unclear' rather than low or high risk, and it did not examine effects on depression, anxiety or distress, so it can say nothing about those. Full appraisal from the full text; strong on design and directly on the claim.

affiliations: School of Life and Medical Sciences
sources.harvard: Jauhar, S., Laws, K. R. & McKenna, P. J. (2019) CBT for schizophrenia: a critical viewpoint. *Psychological Medicine*, 49 (8): 1233-1236. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0033291718004166 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: no primary recruitment; reviews meta-analyses and large RCTs of CBT in schizophrenia and related psychoses
sources.perspective: psychiatry and clinical psychology / critical editorial review of meta-analyses and large RCTs
sources.title: CBT for schizophrenia: a critical viewpoint
sources.strength_why: An editorial 'critical viewpoint', not an independent synthesis: it reports effect sizes drawn from other meta-analyses, one of which is the authors' own (Jauhar et al., 2014), and it has no protocol, no search strategy and no risk-of-bias assessment of its own. It can establish that the pooled effect of CBTp on positive symptoms in meta-analyses published since 2014 lies in the small range, that the effect attenuates under blinding, and that these authors read the evidence as not supporting CBTp for negative symptoms or relapse prevention. It cannot stand as the source of an effect-size figure, because every number in it is secondary; for those, cite Jauhar et al. (2014), British Journal of Psychiatry, 204 (1): 20-29, directly. Indicative rather than moderate because of the publication type and the authors' declared position in the controversy.

(2018) Cognitive behavioural therapy plus standard care versus standard care plus other psychosocial treatments for people with schizophrenia. *Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews*, (11): CD008712. sources.perspective: clinical psychology / Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis with GRADE
sources.dataset: Cochrane Schizophrenia Group Study-Based Register of Trials (to 6 March 2017)
sources.title: Cognitive behavioural therapy plus standard care versus standard care plus other psychosocial treatments for people with schizophrenia
sources.strength_why: A Cochrane review with a registered protocol, a specialist trials register searched without language or publication-status limits, independent duplicate screening and extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE rating: the strongest design in the corpus for a treatment question. What it establishes is narrow and often misread: it compares CBT against OTHER psychosocial therapies as add-ons, not against standard care alone, and it found no clear difference on relapse, rehospitalisation, mental state, death, social functioning or quality of life. It therefore cannot be cited for the size of CBTp's effect against treatment-as-usual, and the authors themselves rate the evidence as mainly low or very low quality. Strong on design; the fit to the claim it is currently being used for is poor.

sources.perspective: psychiatric epidemiology / systematic review and meta-regression of incidence studies
sources.title: International incidence of psychotic disorders, 2002-17: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PROSPERO-registered systematic review (CRD42018086800) screening 56,721 records to 177 included studies, with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression that tests study method as an explanation for the variation it finds. It can establish the pooled incidence of psychotic disorders, the size of the male and ethnic-minority excess, and that part of the geographical variation is an artefact of case-ascertainment design. It cannot establish causes, and heterogeneity was extreme (I-squared at or above 98.5%), which means the pooled rate of 26.6 per 100,000 person-years is a summary of a very dispersed distribution rather than a figure that describes any particular place.

sources.perspective: developmental psychopathology / neuroscience narrative review
sources.title: Dysplasticity, metaplasticity, and schizophrenia: Implications for risk, illness, and novel interventions.
sources.strength_why: A theoretical synthesis, not a study: it can establish that a coherent 'dysplastic' model exists in the peer-reviewed literature and can supply the critical-period vocabulary for discussing when risk converts to onset, but it cannot evidence any individual causal link, because every empirical claim in it is a secondary citation. Used here as FOUNDATIONAL conceptual framing rather than as current evidence; at eleven years old its empirical substrate predates the 2022 GWAS and the current CHR transition meta-analyses already in this corpus. The tier is indicative because it is a theory paper by authors with authority in the field, with no primary data of its own.

sources.strength_why: A population-based first-episode incidence study using Bayesian hierarchical models with spatially structured neighbourhood random effects, which is the appropriate design for this question, and it separates three correlated exposures that are usually confounded: income inequality (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.04-1.49 per SD), absolute deprivation (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.08-1.51) and population density (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.00-1.41), each independently associated with non-affective psychosis after standardising for individual age, sex, ethnicity and socioeconomic status. It is the only source in the corpus in which deprivation predicts PSYCHOSIS rather than general psychopathology, which is precisely the hole in `e1-predispose`. It CANNOT establish causation, and cannot separate social causation from social drift — people with emerging psychosis may move into deprived areas. The density interval reaches 1.00, no neighbourhood-level variation was found for the AFFECTIVE psychoses, and it is a single city over two years with 427 cases, so the neighbourhood-level estimates rest on small numbers per area.

sources.strength_why: A prospective community cohort in rural south India reporting that 70.6% (95% CI 64.35-76.95) achieved clinical remission and 69.6% (95% CI 63.29-76.07) a satisfactory outcome after about four years of ensured continuous antipsychotics plus low-intensity psychoeducation, with disability falling from 66.7% to 27.3% of the cohort. It CANNOT support an efficacy claim: there is no control group, no randomisation and no comparison period, so remission cannot be attributed to the intervention rather than to natural course, regression to the mean or ascertainment; the two components are bundled and cannot be separated; n = 201 in one taluk; and the published abstract is garbled at the disability p-value ('PInterpretation'), so that statistic is NOT recorded here. Indicative because the design cannot carry more.

sources.strength_why: A pre-registered (OSF 8mz7a), PRISMA-ScR/JBI-compliant scoping review of three databases to August 2023, with independent dual title/abstract and full-text screening and third-judge adjudication, mapping 33 primary studies into four clinical-research paradigms. It can establish what the clinical high-risk literature actually measures and with which instruments (CAARMS, SIPS, SPI-A, ERIraos), that CHR-P is operationalised as a help-seeking, subthreshold, functionally impaired state rather than a diagnosis, and that transdiagnostic 'clinical staging' and 'pluripotency' models (CHARMS) are now competing with the psychosis-specific risk paradigm. It cannot establish prevalence, effect size or any causal claim: a scoping review by design does not appraise the quality of the studies it maps or pool their results, and the authors state as their first limitation that 'our study design did not allow for the development of clinical guidelines'. Treated as current rather than foundational: published June 2024, searched to August 2023.

sources.strength_why: A random-effects meta-analysis of 13 studies and 15 647 participants with study and outcome quality assessed using adapted AHRQ and GRADE tools, finding a moderate association between loneliness and psychotic symptoms (r = .32, 95% CI 0.20-0.44) that did not depend on whether loneliness was measured by a single item or a full scale — a measurement-robustness check that matters, because the single-item objection is the obvious one. It can establish that loneliness and psychotic symptoms covary at a clinically meaningful magnitude, which is what lets social isolation be treated as a target rather than a backdrop. It CANNOT establish direction or cause: the authors say explicitly that 'further studies are needed to determine the causal status of this relationship', the included studies are correlational, and heterogeneity is extreme at I-squared = 97.56%, so the pooled r of .32 summarises a very dispersed set of estimates. The authors rate their own evidence 'moderate quality'.

sources.title: Epidemiology of Untreated Psychoses in 3 Diverse Settings in the Global South: The International Research Program on Psychotic Disorders in Diverse Settings (INTREPID II).
sources.strength_why: A population-based incidence study over 3,790,697 person-years in three Global South catchment areas, using identical instruments (SCAN, PPHS) and case-finding across the professional, folk and popular sectors, with leakage studies and interrater reliability reported. It can establish that rates and the demographic and clinical shape of psychosis vary markedly by setting, and that the Global North sex-and-age pattern does not hold everywhere. It cannot establish incidence in the strict sense — the outcome is rate of *untreated* psychosis, a proxy — and the authors say rates where duration of untreated psychosis is long, as in Kancheepuram, are the least accurate proxies.

sources.perspective: psychosis studies and cognitive psychology / Personal View with a lived-experience co-author
sources.title: Artificial intelligence-associated delusions and large language models: risks, mechanisms of delusion co-creation, and safeguarding strategies.
sources.strength_why: A Lancet Psychiatry Personal View, which is a high-visibility venue but an opinion format: no systematic search, no participants, no data of its own. It can establish three things that matter and that no study in the corpus establishes as crisply: that the current evidence indicates reinforcement of existing delusional beliefs rather than induction of de novo psychosis in the absence of vulnerability; that benefit and harm are both on the table, the AI agent sometimes functioning as 'a benign and predictable conversational anchor'; and that the proposed safeguards are UNTESTED, because the authors themselves say the protocols 'must be urgently co-designed with service users and clinicians and tested in clinical trials'. It CANNOT establish prevalence, mechanism or efficacy of anything, and its proposed framework of AI-informed care is a proposal. Indicative on design; its fit to `e2-mechanism`, `e2-evidence` and the education strand of `e2-plan` is excellent.

sources.title: Investigating the neuroanatomical underpinnings of complex PTSD in people with psychosis.
sources.strength_why: A sound primary neuroimaging study that can establish that, within a psychosis population, those additionally meeting ICD-11 cPTSD criteria differ structurally in limbic and prefrontal regions — larger bilateral anterior insula and left parahippocampus, smaller left medial orbitofrontal cortex — with all differences bar hippocampal volume surviving whole-brain correction. It cannot establish direction or cause: it is cross-sectional, and the authors state they cannot tell whether differences reflect cPTSD itself or complex trauma exposure. Antipsychotic and other psychotropic exposure is a stated confounder and differed between groups. Tier is moderate, not strong: n=108 across two separately acquired samples on three different scanners, with correlational post-hoc analyses described by the authors only as trends.

(2022) Immediate and sustained outcomes and moderators associated with metacognitive training for psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *JAMA Psychiatry*, 79 (5): 417-429. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2022.0277 (Accessed 12 October 2026).

sources.perspective: clinical neuropsychology / PRISMA systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression
sources.title: Immediate and sustained outcomes and moderators associated with metacognitive training for psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA-reported meta-analysis of 43 studies, searching eleven databases from 2007 to June 2021, pooling 1816 participants and reporting Hedges g with 95% confidence intervals for proximal and distal outcomes, with effects maintained up to one year. It can establish that a structured intervention aimed at reasoning and cognitive biases reduces delusions (g = 0.69, 95% CI 0.45-0.93) and positive symptoms (g = 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.67) — a directly targeted, durable effect on the symptom class the vignette turns on. It CANNOT establish that it works by changing cognitive biases: the effect on cognitive biases themselves is the smallest significant one in the paper (g = 0.16, 95% CI 0.03-0.29), which undercuts the mechanism the intervention is named for; quality of life was non-significant (g = 0.20, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.47); and the co-developer of the intervention is an author, which is disclosed. Strong on design, with that mechanism finding and that conflict of interest both material.

sources.perspective: psychiatry and psychosocial intervention research / Cochrane systematic review with meta-analysis
sources.title: Family intervention for schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A Cochrane review of 53 RCTs with a very large pooled sample, giving relative risks with 95% confidence intervals and numbers needed to treat, and reporting a substantial reduction in relapse (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.6, NNT 7) alongside improved medication adherence and reduced expressed emotion. It can establish that family intervention is an evidence-based component of a psychosis treatment plan, and it supplies the NNT a plan can be justified with. It CANNOT be read at face value: the authors state the treatment effects 'may be overestimated due to the poor methodological quality' of the trials, the hospital-admission result crosses 1 (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.0), and they note small negative studies may have been missed by the search. It is also NOT first-episode-specific — the population is schizophrenia and schizophrenia-like conditions broadly — and it is a 2010 review, so fifteen years out of date. Moderate rather than strong on the authors' own quality caveat and on fit.

sources.authors: Reiss, F.
sources.harvard: Reiss, F. (2013) Socioeconomic inequalities and mental health problems in children and adolescents: a systematic review. *Social Science & Medicine*, 90: 24-31. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2013.04.026 (Accessed 12 October 2026).

sources.perspective: public health and social epidemiology / systematic review
sources.title: Socioeconomic inequalities and mental health problems in children and adolescents: A systematic review.
sources.strength_why: A systematic review that can establish a consistent inverse gradient between socioeconomic status and mental health problems in children and adolescents — 52 of 55 included studies found it, disadvantaged young people being two to three times more likely to develop mental health problems — and can establish that persistent low SES and declining SES are both worse than transient disadvantage, which is a dose and duration finding the corpus otherwise lacks. It CANNOT establish anything about psychosis: the outcome throughout is 'mental health problems', measured by general psychopathology screens, and the review does not disaggregate psychotic experiences. The author lists publication bias and the diversity of SES and outcome measures as limitations, and states that excluding longitudinal studies of over-18s 'restricted the study's ability to observe causal associations over the life course'. Tier is moderate on quality; its FIT for a psychosis essay is POOR.

sources.perspective: clinical psychiatry / meta-analysis of longitudinal cohorts, with reconstructed Kaplan-Meier survival curves
sources.title: Probability of Transition to Psychosis in Individuals at Clinical High Risk: An Updated Meta-analysis.
sources.strength_why: A PRISMA- and MOOSE-compliant meta-analysis of 130 longitudinal studies and 9222 individuals, with independent data extraction, digitisation of published Kaplan-Meier curves to recover survival data, heterogeneity analysis, study-quality assessment and meta-regression. It can establish, with unusual precision for this literature, what proportion of people meeting clinical high-risk criteria go on to develop psychosis and over what period. It cannot establish what predicts transition in an individual, and it inherits the selection bias of the help-seeking samples that clinical high-risk services recruit, so the rates do not transfer to the general population.

Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.schres.2019.07.047 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 57 patients with psychosis receiving up to 45 sessions of CBTp, secondary analysis of a published trial; recruited in Germany (Hamburg and Marburg)
sources.perspective: clinical psychology / secondary multilevel mediation analysis of weekly repeated measures within a therapy trial
sources.dataset: a previously published CBTp trial (parent trial not identified in the abstract)
sources.title: Fostering coping as a mechanism of symptom change in cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis
sources.strength_why: The only source found so far that tests the direction of the coping-symptom relationship rather than assuming it: weekly self-assessments across up to 45 sessions, analysed by multilevel models, with a reverse model fitted as well, which is the right design for a mechanism question and is why it outranks Strous (2005) and MacAulay & Cohen (2013) for this claim despite being smaller. It establishes temporal precedence in an uncontrolled, within-person, treatment-improvement direction: improvement in coping preceded improvement in suspiciousness, negative symptoms and depression. It cannot establish causation or generalise to exacerbation, because it is a secondary analysis of a single uncontrolled therapy sample of 57 people, all measures are self-report, and the mediator and outcome share method and informant. Indicative on sample size, secondary-analysis status and abstract-only access; the design is the reason it is usable at all.

sources.authors: Sinha, R.
sources.harvard: Sinha, R. (2008) Chronic stress, drug use, and vulnerability to addiction. *Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences*, 1141 (1): 105-130. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1196/annals.1441.030 (Accessed 12 October 2026).

sources.perspective: psychiatry and neuroendocrinology / narrative review across preclinical and human literatures
sources.title: Chronic stress, drug use, and vulnerability to addiction.
sources.strength_why: A single-author narrative review that can establish the shape of the stress-addiction vulnerability account — that chronic stress, child maltreatment and accumulated adversity alter CRF/HPA, autonomic and central noradrenergic systems, and that these alterations act on corticostriatal-limbic motivational and learning systems — and can identify where the primary evidence sits. It cannot establish any specific causal pathway, has no search strategy, and is eighteen years old. Used as FOUNDATIONAL framing for a stress-vulnerability model, not as a current statement of the addiction neuroscience literature. Tier is indicative: authoritative review, no primary data, substantially dated.

sources.title: Psychopathology of schizophrenia in Ljubljana (Slovenia) from 1881 to 2000: changes in the content of delusions in schizophrenia patients related to various sociopolitical, technical and scientific changes
sources.strength_why: A retrospective case-note study of 120 randomly selected first-admission records spanning 120 years, which can show that the thematic content of delusions shifted alongside the arrival of radio and television and alongside political change in Slovenia. It cannot establish that the technology caused the shift, nor that the comparison is like for like, because diagnostic practice, recording conventions and the hospital's catchment all changed across the same period and roughly 20 records represent each 20-year span. Indicative rather than moderate because of the small per-period cell sizes and because the appraisal rests on the abstract alone.

sources.perspective: psychiatric genetics / twin design combined with molecular polygenic scoring
sources.dataset: Swedish Twin Registry; Schizophrenia and Bipolar Twin Study in Sweden (STAR)
sources.title: Polygenic Risk Scores and Twin Concordance for Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder.
sources.strength_why: A twin study that brings two independent methods to bear on the same question — classical twin modelling and molecular polygenic risk scores — in a national twin registry, which is why it can speak to heritability and to whether the molecular and twin estimates agree. It can establish a twin heritability estimate for psychosis of 0.73 and show that polygenic risk predicted co-twin concordance. It cannot support a precise heritability figure: the genotyped sample is small at 292 twins and the 95% confidence interval on the headline estimate runs from 0.30 to 1.00, which is almost the whole admissible range.

(2005) Longitudinal assessment of coping abilities at exacerbation and stabilization in schizophrenia. *Comprehensive Psychiatry*, 46 (3): 167-175. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.comppsych.2004.07.035 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: patients with schizophrenia assessed at exacerbation (n=237) and again at stabilization (n=148) over a 16-month follow-up; hospital services in Israel
sources.perspective: psychiatry / prospective observational cohort with repeated measures and multiple regression
sources.title: Longitudinal assessment of coping abilities at exacerbation and stabilization in schizophrenia
sources.strength_why: A genuinely longitudinal clinical cohort - 237 patients assessed in an acute exacerbation and 148 of them again at stabilization across 16 months - with a validated coping instrument and a wide battery of clinical and psychosocial measures, which is a stronger design than anything else currently available to this project on coping in psychosis. What it establishes is that emotion-oriented coping is used more during exacerbation than during stabilization, and that emotional distress, self-efficacy and social support predict coping style at both phases. What it cannot establish is the direction the argument needs: coping is the DEPENDENT variable in every regression reported, symptom severity is a predictor of it, and symptom severity accounts for only 3.5% of the variance in emotion-oriented coping and 5.5-9% in task-oriented coping. Moderate on design; attrition from 237 to 148 is 37.6% and unexplained in the abstract, and the record is abstract-only.

sources.perspective: clinical psychology / expert narrative overview and implementation argument
sources.title: Cognitive Remediation Is an Evidence-Based Psychological Therapy: Isn't It Time It Was Treated Like One?
sources.strength_why: An advocacy-framed expert overview, current at 2025, that can establish that cognitive remediation is treated in the field as an evidence-based intervention, that it uses therapeutic formulation in the way other psychological therapies do, and that it is nonetheless inconsistently included in clinical guidelines. It cannot carry an effect size or a recovery claim of its own, because the authors state plainly that they 'have not systematically reviewed the literature but have used expert knowledge and reviews by others'. The authors are among the field's principal proponents, which is relevant to how its conclusions are read. Tier is indicative: a non-systematic review with a stated position.

sources.harvard: Teferra, S., Shibre, T., Fekadu, A., Medhin, G., Wakwoya, A., Alem, A. & Jacobsson, L. (2012) Five-year clinical course and outcome of schizophrenia in Ethiopia. *Schizophrenia Research*, 136 (1-3): 137-142. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.schres.2011.10.021 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 321 people with schizophrenia identified by screening 68 378 adults aged 15-49 in rural Ethiopia (Butajira); 74.9% had chronic illness at entry and 89.6% were treatment naive
sources.perspective: social psychiatry and global mental health / population-based prospective cohort with 5-year follow-up
sources.title: Five-year clinical course and outcome of schizophrenia in Ethiopia.
sources.strength_why: A population-based prospective cohort with five-year follow-up, built by screening 68 378 adults rather than by sampling clinic attenders, in a setting where 89.6% of cases were treatment naive at entry — a design that is now almost impossible to repeat and that directly tests the long-standing claim of better schizophrenia outcomes in low-income countries. It can establish that the WHO 'better outcome in developing countries' finding does not hold here: 45% were continuously symptomatic, 30.3% had a continuous psychotic episode and only about 20% had continuous remission, and it can establish that being on antipsychotic treatment for at least half the follow-up predicted longer remission (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.12-4.62). It CANNOT establish that treatment caused the better outcome: the treatment exposure is observational, so reverse causation and confounding by severity are open, and the cohort was largely chronic at entry so it is not a first-episode study. Moderate: strong design for its question, non-first-episode population, observational treatment comparison.

sources.authors: Torres-Rodríguez, A., Griffiths, M. D. & Carbonell, X.
sources.harvard: Torres-Rodríguez, A., Griffiths, M. D. & Carbonell, X. (2018) The treatment of Internet Gaming Disorder: a brief overview of the PIPATIC program. *International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction*, 16 (4): 1000-1015. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11469-017-9825-0 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: no participants in this paper; the programme is designed for 12- to 18-year-olds with Internet Gaming Disorder, developed in Spain
sources.perspective: clinical psychology / treatment-programme design paper
sources.title: The treatment of Internet Gaming Disorder: a brief overview of the PIPATIC program.
sources.strength_why: A programme-description paper that can establish what a manualised multi-module adolescent intervention looks like in practice — six modules over six months and twenty-two 45-minute weekly sessions for both individual and family work, designed against CONSORT reporting standards — and is therefore usable as a TEMPLATE for the architecture of a treatment plan. It cannot establish that the programme works: the authors' own word for their outcome data is 'preliminary', and no controlled comparison is reported in this paper. Its population is adolescents with Internet Gaming Disorder, not psychosis, so the FIT is structural rather than evidential. Tier is indicative: a design paper with preliminary, uncontrolled outcome data.

sources.authors: Trubetskoy, V., Pardiñas, A. F., Qi, T. and 300 further authors, Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium
sources.population: up to 76,755 individuals with schizophrenia and 243,649 control individuals, two-stage genome-wide association study
sources.perspective: statistical genetics / genome-wide association study with fine-mapping and functional genomics
sources.title: Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A two-stage genome-wide association study of up to 76,755 cases and 243,649 controls reporting 287 distinct genome-wide significant loci, with fine-mapping and functional genomic follow-up prioritising 120 genes, published in Nature. It can establish that schizophrenia liability is highly polygenic, that the associated variation is concentrated in genes expressed in central-nervous-system neurons rather than other tissues, and that common and rare variant signals converge. It cannot establish individual-level risk prediction, cannot identify a cause in any one person, and because the heritability figure of 60-80% that opens the paper is cited from prior twin work rather than estimated here, that figure is a secondary citation if used.

(2012) Childhood adversities increase the risk of psychosis: a meta-analysis of patient-control, prospective- and cross-sectional cohort studies. *Schizophrenia Bulletin*, 38 (4): 661-671. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbs050 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: 41 studies: 18 case-control (2048 psychotic patients, 1856 non-psychiatric controls), 10 prospective/quasi-prospective (n=41,803), 8 population-based cross-sectional (n=35,546)
sources.perspective: psychology / epidemiology, meta-analysis of observational designs
sources.title: Childhood adversities increase the risk of psychosis: a meta-analysis of patient-control, prospective- and cross-sectional cohort studies.
sources.strength_why: A meta-analysis pooling three different observational designs, which can establish that the adversity-psychosis association is large, consistent and not an artefact of any single design: the overall OR was 2.78 (95% CI 2.34-3.31) and it held separately in prospective studies (OR 2.75, 95% CI 2.17-3.47). It cannot establish causation, cannot separate the timing or dose of adversity, and the authors state that heterogeneity was substantial for every outcome. The tier is strong because it is a design-triangulated meta-analysis with sensitivity analyses restricted to adjusted estimates, not because of its size alone.

sources.authors: Vassos, E., Pedersen, C. B., Murray, R. M., Collier, D. A. & Lewis, C. M.
sources.harvard: Vassos, E., Pedersen, C. B., Murray, R. M., Collier, D. A. & Lewis, C. M. (2012) Meta-analysis of the association of urbanicity with schizophrenia. *Schizophrenia Bulletin*, 38 (6): 1118-1123. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1093/schbul/sbs096 (Accessed 12 October 2026).
sources.population: studies reporting incidence of schizophrenia or non-affective psychosis by level of urbanicity; number of included studies not stated in the abstract
sources.perspective: genetic epidemiology / meta-analysis with simulated individual data points and logistic regression
sources.title: Meta-analysis of the association of urbanicity with schizophrenia.
sources.strength_why: A meta-analysis that reframes the urbanicity-schizophrenia association as a linear dose-response on the log odds rather than a most-urban-versus-most-rural comparison, estimating risk in the most urban environment as 2.37 times that in the most rural. It can establish that the association is graded by degree of urbanicity rather than being a city-versus-country dichotomy, which is what makes it useful for a predisposing-factor argument. It cannot establish causation or distinguish social causation from social drift, and the abstract does not state how many studies were included or give a confidence interval for the headline 2.37 figure, so the precision of that estimate cannot be judged from this record.

Tier is moderate: systematic method, substantial heterogeneity, stated limits.

It establishes diagnostic nomenclature and criteria, and it is the right citation for a definition, for the boundary of a diagnostic category, and for the statement that something is or is not a recognised diagnostic entity - which Essay 2 needs. sources.strength_why: A seven-year follow-up of a randomised trial in remitted first-episode psychosis with 80.5% of the original randomised sample located, reporting that the dose-reduction/discontinuation arm had twice the recovery rate of the maintenance arm (40.4% versus 17.6%, OR 3.49, P = .01), driven by functional rather than symptomatic remission. It CANNOT bear a recommendation: the randomisation governed only the first 18 months and treatment after the 2-year trial was 'at the discretion of the clinician', so the seven-year comparison is observational in all but name; it was an open (unblinded) trial; 111 of 257 eligible patients refused, which is a severe selection problem; n is 103 and the primary outcome was not the original trial's; and the authors say 'additional studies are necessary before these results are incorporated into general practice'. Moderate, and the reason is the 18-month randomisation window, not the finding.

Moderate on the authors' own effect-size caveat and the inpatient setting, which is a poor match for a college student in the community.

sources.title: Emotional support or problem-solving? A randomized controlled trial of function-specific AI chatbots for digital stress in college students.
sources.strength_why: A genuine three-arm randomised controlled trial with a waitlist control in the vignette's population — university students, selected for elevated digital stress — which is a design the AI-and-mental-health corpus otherwise does not contain at all, and with Chinese participants, which the corpus badly needs. It can establish that a 14-day self-guided generative-AI chatbot can reduce specific dimensions of digital stress, and that function matters: the emotional-support bot reduced availability stress, approval anxiety, social comparison stress and fear of missing out, while the problem-solving bot was better at reducing online vigilance. It CANNOT bear weight on psychosis: there is no psychosis or psychosis-risk outcome anywhere in it, the sample is 99 across three arms so roughly 33 per cell, the follow-up is 14 days, and 'both interventions significantly alleviated anxiety symptoms, whereas effects on depressive symptoms were not significant' — a split result the essay should report rather than round up. Indicative: strong design, very small, very short, and wrong outcome for the claim it would be asked to support.

sources.strength_why: The dedicated first-episode evidence synthesis for acute antipsychotic treatment: 19 RCTs, 12 drugs, 2669 participants, with SMDs and ORs and 95% CIs, searching seven databases plus ClinicalTrials.gov without language restriction. It can establish that haloperidol is a suboptimal first choice in first-episode schizophrenia, that differences between second-generation drugs are small, and — the finding that matters most for a treatment plan — that 'the choice of treatment should be guided primarily by side-effects'. Moderate rather than strong on the authors' own quality assessment of the underlying trials.

sources.strength_why: A theoretical paper, not an empirical study, and the originating statement of the stress-vulnerability model of schizophrenia: it is cited because it is the source of the concept, which is exactly the use foundational work is for. Its age is not a weakness here - a 1977 paper is the correct citation for a 1977 idea, and citing a 2020s textbook for it instead would be a weaker reference, not a stronger one. What it cannot do is carry any empirical weight: it predates neuroimaging, molecular genetics and every modern incidence study, so any claim about the size or mechanism of a risk factor must be cited to current evidence and never to this. Indicative per the tier definition for foundational theory papers; the rating is of evidential weight, not of importance.

clips.note: RESOLVED, but the claim has to be REWORDED, and the rewording is not cosmetic. Boge's sentence - that differences in coping ability play a role in symptom EXACERBATION - is not supportable. MacAulay & Cohen (2013) does not study exacerbation at all (cross-sectional, 27 patients, headline null, and Boge's sentence traces to MacAulay's own introduction). Strous et al. (2005) is genuinely longitudinal but runs the arrow the OTHER WAY: every regression has coping as the dependent variable and symptoms as a predictor of it, severity explaining 3.5% to 9% of coping variance, and the authors conclude coping [quoted wording withheld]. Using Strous here would reverse its own causal framing - the same error made three times already in this chain. What IS evidenced is narrower and still enough: Schlier et al. (2020) found that [quoted wording withheld], and fitted the reverse model too - improvement in suspiciousness or positive symptoms did NOT predict later coping improvement, though negative symptoms and depression did. So write coping as a MODIFIABLE MAINTAINING FACTOR whose improvement precedes symptom improvement within therapy, not as a deficit that drives exacerbation in untreated psychosis. Four limits travel with it: 57 German outpatients, one group, both measures self-reported by the same person, and individualised positive symptoms conspicuously absent from what coping improvement preceded. Also note Strous's honest use, which is real: coping is STATE-DEPENDENT, emotion-focused coping rising in acute phases - so a coping assessment taken during an acute presentation is measuring a moving target, which is a point the formulation section can use. INDEPENDENCE: Schlier's senior author is Tania Lincoln, who is also Lincoln & Peters (2019) and Lincoln & Heibach (2017), so four links in what looked like a six-source theoretical chain come from one Hamburg group.
